questions.question: What specific rule does verse 1 establish about when a husband may pronounce divorce?
options: A) He may pronounce it at any time, including during the wife's menstrual period
B) He must pronounce it at the start of a period of purity in which no intercourse has occurred, so the iddah can begin and be counted accurately
C) He must wait until the iddah has already ended before pronouncing divorce
D) He may pronounce it only after consulting a judge
questions.explanation: The verse commands that divorce be initiated at the beginning of a clean period (tuhr) in which no intercourse has taken place, so the three-month waiting period can commence clearly and be counted accurately. This ruling was revealed in direct response to the incident of Ibn Umar, who divorced his wife during her menstrual period and was firmly corrected by the Prophet, as recorded by Imam al-Bukhari and Muslim.

questions.question: True or false: According to verse 1, a divorced wife has the right to remain in the marital home throughout the iddah, and the husband is forbidden from expelling her.
questions.explanation: Verse 1 establishes three protective housing rulings: the wife must not be expelled from the marital home, she must not leave voluntarily, and the only exception is if she commits a clear immorality. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen specifically warned that the widespread cultural practice of immediately sending the wife to her family's home upon divorce violates this explicit Quranic command.

questions.question: Which classical scholar preserved a narration that Ali ibn Abi Talib said a man should have two just witnesses when divorcing or taking back his wife, presenting this as a direct Quranic obligation?
options: A) Imam al-Tabari, in his discussion of the phrase 'retain them according to acceptable terms'
B) Ibn Kathir, in his Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, citing narrations attributed to Ali and Ibn Abbas
C) Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, in his analysis of the surah's rhetorical structure in Mafatih al-Ghayb
D) Imam al-Suyuti, in his Tafsir al-Jalalayn
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir gives great weight to the stipulation of two just witnesses in verse 2, citing the view attributed to Ali ibn Abi Talib that 'if a man divorces or returns his wife, he should have two just men as witnesses, as Allah commands.' Ibn Kathir treats this as a binding Quranic obligation backed by Companion authority.

questions.question: True or false: The promise in verse 3 that Allah will provide 'from where one does not reckon' means a person of taqwa may abandon worldly effort and simply wait for provision to arrive.
questions.explanation: Fakhr al-Din al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb explicitly distinguishes tawakkul from fatalism, explaining it means taking all necessary worldly steps while anchoring the heart in certainty that outcomes belong to Allah alone. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen similarly notes that the Prophet ploughed fields, conducted trade, and fought battles — tawakkul is an inner orientation, not a substitute for action.

questions.question: Verse 4 specifies different iddah rulings for different categories of women. What is the waiting period for a pregnant divorced woman?
options: A) Three months, identical to the rule for post-menopausal women
B) Four months and ten days
C) Until the child is born, regardless of how much time remains in the pregnancy
D) One full year from the date of divorce
questions.explanation: Verse 4 states that for pregnant women the iddah extends until they give birth, making childbirth — not the passage of months — the event that terminates the waiting period. Ibn Kathir records that Ubayy ibn Ka'b asked the Prophet about the iddah for women who do not menstruate, and this very verse was revealed in direct response.

questions.question: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran singles out verse 6's prohibition on harming divorced wives through oppressive living conditions. What does he say this prohibition reveals about the nature of Islamic law?
options: A) That housing disputes must be resolved by a community elder before any divorce can proceed
B) That using economic and domestic power to torment a vulnerable person is not merely a legal offence but a violation of the divine moral order itself
C) That the wife forfeits housing rights if she was the one who requested the divorce
D) That the husband's housing obligation automatically ends on the first day of the iddah
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb writes that the prohibition on harming women to make their lives difficult is a moral declaration, not merely a legal restriction — using economic and domestic power to torment a vulnerable person violates the divine order. He observes that when a marriage breaks down, divine law intervenes precisely at the point of greatest vulnerability for the woman and any unborn child.

questions.question: How did the scholars of the Salaf, as recorded by Imam al-Tabari, understand the word 'atat' used to describe the defiant communities in verse 8?
options: A) As accidental ignorance, implying those communities simply had not received clear guidance
B) As wilful, insolent defiance of commands that were clearly known — distinguishing it from ignorant error
C) As military rebellion against prophets only, not as violations of family or social law
D) As gradual religious drift caused by poverty and hardship
questions.explanation: Imam al-Tabari records the view of the early scholars that 'atw' (the root of 'atat') signifies open, wilful defiance rather than ignorant error. This distinction matters because ignorance may be answered with guidance, but deliberate arrogance meets with severe accounting and punishment — which is precisely the fate described for those communities in verse 8.

questions.question: True or false: Ibn Kathir interprets the phrase 'they tasted the evil consequence of their conduct' in verse 9 as meaning that divine punishment was an arbitrary imposition unconnected to what those communities had chosen to do.
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir treats verse 9 as a statement of moral causation: the Arabic 'wabala amriha' conveys that the destruction was the direct, inevitable result of the communities' own chosen defiance, not an arbitrary external event. Using the image of 'tasting,' the Quran communicates that punishment is as immediate and personal as a physical sensation, not a distant or disconnected consequence.

questions.question: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir describes a key architectural feature of Surah At-Talaq that illuminates the contrast between the fate of believers and disbelievers. What is that feature?
options: A) The surah opens and closes with an identical verse about taqwa, creating a perfect ring structure
B) The movement from minutely detailed family law in verses 1-7 to the eternal reward of Paradise in verse 11 shows that obedience in private life is the path from darkness into divine light
C) Verse 11 lists the specific punishments awaiting those who violated the divorce rulings of verse 1
D) The surah uses the same Arabic root for both the darknesses of disobedience and the punishment of past nations
questions.explanation: Al-Zuhayli describes the surah's movement from the most practical legislative detail — housing standards, iddah timing, financial proportionality — to the eternal promise of gardens beneath which rivers flow as a masterpiece of Quranic literary architecture. Those who follow divine commands in family life are precisely the believers whom the Messenger leads 'from darknesses into the light,' with Allah perfecting their provision forever, in contrast to those who defy His commands and end in total loss.
